bib.title: Deep Learning is Not So Mysterious or Different

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Deep Learning is Not So Mysterious or Different", Andrew Gordon Wilson (NYU). ICML 2025 (Proceedings of the 42nd ICML, Vancouver, PMLR 267). arXiv:2503.02113v2, 10 Jul 2025. It is a position paper.

COVERAGE: All 101036 chars read, including appendices A to D and Table 1. The reference list (roughly chars 66000-88000) was skimmed only for origins. All text extracted cleanly. The figure panels are only partly readable as text (axis ticks). I did not run the figures script, so captions come from the extraction.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: Benign overfitting, double descent and the success of overparametrization are not specific to neural networks. They are described by PAC-Bayes and countable-hypothesis bounds, which predate deep learning.
  number: none
  setup: argument plus toy demonstrations (polynomial, linear random features, GP, ResNet).
  quote: "none of these phenomena are distinct to neural networks, or particularly mysterious." and "understanding deep learning does not require re-thinking generalization, and it never did."
  where: Section 1, p.2

- claim: Soft inductive bias is the unifying principle. Use a flexible hypothesis space with a soft preference for simple solutions that fit the data, instead of restricting the space.
  number: none
  setup: conceptual. Examples are a polynomial with order-dependent regularization, residual pathway priors (soft equivariance), and overparametrization.
  quote: "rather than restricting the hypothesis space to avoid overfitting, embrace a flexible hypothesis space, with a soft preference for simpler solutions that are consistent with the data."
  where: Abstract; Section 2

- claim: A 150th-order polynomial with order-dependent regularization fits simple and structured data reasonably and also fits pure noise perfectly. So it shows benign overfitting.
  number: 150th order
  setup: Fig 1(a-c). Data from sin(x)cos(x^2), x+cos(pi x), and N(0,1) noise. Penalty is sum_j 2^j w_j^2 (Appendix D).
  quote: "A 150th order polynomial with order-dependent regularization reasonably describes (a) simple and (b) complex structured data, while also being able to perfectly fit (c) pure noise."
  where: Fig 1 caption, p.2; App D

- claim: A Gaussian process reproduces the Zhang et al. CIFAR-10 noisy-label experiment. It fits with no training error and generalization degrades steadily as more labels are altered. The marginal likelihood of both the GP and the ResNet falls as more labels are altered, which matches PAC-Bayes bounds.
  number: label alterations up to 25k (GP) and 50k (ResNet-20) of the CIFAR-10 training set. Fig 1(d)(e) axis ticks only.
  setup: GP with RBF kernel; PreResNet-20 with isotropic prior and Laplace marginal likelihood; adapted from Wilson & Izmailov (2020).
  quote: "A Gaussian process exactly reproduces the CIFAR-10 results in Zhang et al. (2016), perfectly fitting noisy labels, but still achieving reasonable generalization."
  where: Fig 1, p.2; Sec 4, p.7; App D

- claim: Generalization bound recipe. Expected risk is at most empirical risk plus a compressibility term. Kolmogorov complexity is upper-bounded by the stored model filesize, so large but compressible models generalize. The recipe is train, measure training loss, measure filesize, substitute into the bound.
  number: none (formula)
  setup: countable-hypothesis bound with a Solomonoff prior. Risk bounded in [a, a+Delta]; holds with probability at least 1-delta.
  quote: "R(h) ≤ ˆR(h) + ∆ s log 1/P(h) + log 1/δ / 2n" and "(i) train a model to find hypothesis h∗, using any optimizer; (ii) measure the empirical risk ˆR(h∗) (e.g., training loss); (iii) measure the filesize of the stored model for C(h∗); (iv) substitute Eq. (4) into Eq. (2)."
  where: Sec 3.1, pp.5-6; Eq 1-4

- claim: These bounds are non-vacuous, and sometimes tight, for large networks.
  number: 16.6% test-error bound on CIFAR-10, with at least 95% probability, for a model with millions of parameters. Non-vacuous for LLMs with billions of parameters.
  setup: Lotfi et al. (2022a) for CIFAR-10; Lotfi et al. (2024b) and Finzi et al. (2025) for LLMs. The bounds are cited, not re-run here.
  quote: "Lotfi et al. (2022a) upper bound the classification error of a model with millions of parameters on CIFAR-10 at 16.6% with at least 95% probability, which is fairly respectable performance on this benchmark."
  where: Sec 3.1, p.6

- claim: Larger models can have a stronger compression or simplicity bias. They have fewer effective parameters after training, and bounds can tighten with size. Flat, compressible solutions take up a larger share of the hypothesis space as parameters increase.
  number: none
  setup: Maddox et al. (2020) measured Hessian effective dimensionality. Goldblum et al. (2024) studied LLMs. Lotfi et al. (2022a; 2024) bounds. The author calls the cause "a fascinating open question" with only clues so far.
  quote: "Maddox et al. (2020) found that larger models after training had fewer effective parameters than smaller models" and "recent bounds become tighter, not looser, with larger models."
  where: Sec 3.1 p.6; Sec 5.2, p.8

- claim: Double descent is old and not deep-learning specific. It dates to Opper et al. (1989), and Belkin et al. (2019) already showed it for random forests and random-feature models. It can be reproduced with a linear random-feature model, and effective dimensionality tracks the second descent.
  number: 1989 (original date); Fig 1(g) uses 200 features on the axis and alpha=10; Fig 1(f) uses ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100 with alpha=1.
  setup: Linear model Xw=y with features y+eps, eps~N(0,1). Second descent explained via the Marchenko-Pastur distribution, minimum-norm least squares, and variance error falling once d>n.
  quote: "The original introduction of double descent surprisingly dates back three decades earlier, at least to Opper et al. (1989)" and "Once d > n, the model can interpolate the data perfectly with infinitely many parameter settings w."
  where: Sec 6, pp.9-10; Fig 1; App D

- claim: In the second descent every model fits the data perfectly, so extra flexibility cannot explain the gain. Instead flat, compressible solutions grow in volume and become easier to find, and effective dimensionality drops.
  number: none
  setup: ResNet-18 with increasing width, trained to convergence, CIFAR-100 cross-entropy loss (Maddox et al. 2020 setup).
  quote: "in this second descent, all models achieve a perfect fit to the data, and therefore increased flexibility cannot be the reason that the models with more parameters achieve better generalization."
  where: Sec 6, p.9

- claim: The implicit bias of SGD is not necessary for generalization. Full-batch gradient descent does nearly as well, and "guess and check" (random sampling until the loss is low) is competitive.
  number: none ("nearly as well", "competitive", "similar or only slightly worse")
  setup: Geiping et al. (2021) with large residual networks; Chiang et al. (2022). Cited results, not run here. The author notes SGD has useful biases and is far more practical.
  quote: "Geiping et al. (2021) found that full-batch gradient descent could perform nearly as well as SGD for training large residual networks, and Chiang et al. (2022) further showed that even guess and check ... can provide competitive generalization with stochastic training."
  where: Sec 5.2, p.9; Sec 9, p.13

- claim: Bias-variance "trade-off" is a misnomer. The U-shaped curve comes from constrained models having high bias and unconstrained models having high variance. Models with low bias and low variance exist, such as order-dependent polynomials and ensembles. Textbook zero-training-error warnings reflect this.
  number: none
  setup: argument. Bishop (2006, Ch 3, p.168) is called out. The "intermediate-order" marginal-likelihood result is called "an artifact of a bad prior" because it uses an isotropic prior.
  quote: "But “trade-off” is a misnomer: models such as our order-dependent polynomial in Section 2, or ensembles (Bishop, 2006; Wilson & Izmailov, 2020), can have low bias and low variance."
  where: Sec 7, p.10; Sec 2, p.4

- claim: Rademacher complexity, VC dimension and fat-shattering penalize the size of the hypothesis space (its ability to fit noise), so they give uninformative bounds for benign overfitting. PAC-Bayes and countable bounds pass the Zhang et al. randomized-label test.
  number: none
  setup: Table 1 compares the bounds. Rademacher is "2000s", VC and fat-shattering "1990s", PAC-Bayes "1990s", finite hypothesis "1980s". Formulas are R(h) ≤ R̂(h)+2R_n(H)+3sqrt(log(2/δ)/2n) and O(sqrt(d log n / n)).
  quote: "Does not explain overparametrization, benign overfitting, or double descent." (Table 1, Rademacher and VC rows)
  where: Sec 3.3; App B; Table 1, p.21

- claim: Soft equivariance (residual pathway priors) matches a hard-constrained model when the symmetry is exact, and beats it when the symmetry is approximate or absent. Trained vision transformers can be more translation-equivariant than ConvNets, because aliasing breaks ConvNet equivariance.
  number: none
  setup: Finzi et al. (2021) RPP; Gruver et al. (2023) Lie-derivative equivariance measurement. Cited results.
  quote: "Surprisingly, vision transformers after training can be even more translation equivariant than convolutional neural networks (Gruver et al., 2023)!"
  where: Sec 2, p.4

- claim: What really is distinctive about deep learning is representation learning (an adaptive basis, learned similarity or kernel), universality and in-context learning, and mode connectivity. Even these are not entirely unique, since deep kernel learning and tree-ensemble mode connectivity exist.
  number: none
  setup: Garipov et al. (2018) ResNet-164 on CIFAR-100 for mode connectivity (Fig 7). Gruver et al. (2024) for LLM zero-shot time-series forecasting.
  quote: "Representation learning is largely what sets neural networks apart from other model classes." and "a standard LLM pre-trained on text completion can surprisingly make competitive zero-shot time series forecasts relative to purpose-built time series models"
  where: Sec 8.1-8.3, pp.11-13

- claim: Model-size and optimizer prescriptions. A large model with a simplicity bias can do well at every data size, and parameter sharing can be a poor principle for compute-optimal scaling. Scaling laws and grokking also appear in linear models.
  number: Fig 5 uses 10 to 100 training samples, 100 refits, 100 test samples.
  setup: Fig 5 compares a 2nd-order, a 15th-order and a regularized 15th-order polynomial (penalty sum 0.01*2^j... as printed "0.012j2w2j") on three target functions. The regularized 15th-order one is "as good or better than all other models for all data sizes".
  quote: "A large model can achieve good performance for all data sizes, as long as it combined with a simplicity bias, as we saw in the polynomial example."
  where: Sec 9, p.13; Fig 5, p.5; App D

LIMITS
- The author does not claim deep learning is fully understood. He says he is "not aiming to argue that deep learning is fully understood" and is not assigning historical priority.
- Why larger models get a stronger compression bias is called "a fascinating open question." The author says "we are still in the early stages of understanding precisely how and why scale and other factors influence the implicit regularization".
- Flatness is not parametrization invariant, and flatter solutions do not always generalize better (Dinh et al. 2017). Effective dimensionality is intuition, not a bound.
- Kolmogorov complexity cannot separate randomness-driven incompressibility from structural complexity. The author wants to move beyond it.
- PAC-Bayes bounds are descriptive and only as tight as the prior. A mismatched prior gives a loose bound.
- Restriction biases can still help for computation, such as sparsity and parameter sharing. The setting is idealized, with computation treated as free.
- Almost all evidence is cited from prior work (Lotfi, Maddox, Goldblum, Finzi, Geiping) or toy models. Only Fig 1 and Fig 5 are experiments, and Figs 2 to 4 are conceptual. There are no new large-scale results, and no numbers for how loose the bounds are on LLMs.
- The Fig 1(f) caption says ResNet-18 but the text says CIFAR-100 cross-entropy, while Appendix D only says "ResNet-18 with increasing layer width".
- Grokking and scaling laws are explicitly out of scope, with only a pointer to Finzi et al. (2025).

BUILDS ON: PAC-Bayes (McAllester 1999; Catoni 2007; Dziugaite & Roy 2017; Germain et al. 2016). Countable hypothesis bounds (Valiant 1984; Shalev-Shwartz & Ben-David 2014; Lotfi et al. 2024a). Solomonoff 1964 and Kolmogorov complexity. Zhang et al. 2016/2021 (the claim being rebutted). Belkin et al. 2019 and Nakkiran et al. 2020 (double descent). Bartlett et al. 2020 (benign overfitting in linear regression). Maddox et al. 2020 (effective dimensionality). Wilson & Izmailov 2020 (marginal likelihood, GP replication). Rasmussen & Ghahramani 2000. Finzi et al. 2021 (RPP). Goldblum et al. 2024. Opper et al. 1989. Garipov et al. 2018. Geiping et al. 2021. Chiang et al. 2022. MacKay 1995/2003.

CODE: none. Formulas in the text only. Eq 1 is the countable hypothesis bound (p.5). Eq 2 is the Solomonoff-prior version with K(h|A) log 2. Eq 4 is log 1/P(h) ≤ C(h) log 2 + 2 log C(h). The effective-dimensionality formula is on p.6, Sec 3.2. The Appendix C proof is a Hoeffding inequality plus a union bound.

FIGURES (from extraction; no figures script run)
- Fig 1, p.2: top row shows benign overfitting (polynomial, GP and ResNet on CIFAR-10 noisy labels). Bottom row shows double descent (ResNet-18, linear random features) with effective dimensionality. It is the best single summary of the paper.
- Fig 2, p.3: generalization bound = empirical risk + compression term, with LLM bounds from Lotfi et al.
- Fig 3 and Fig 4: soft versus restriction bias, and training dynamics under each. Fig 6: the volume of flat generalizing solutions grows with parameters.
- Fig 5, p.5: regularized 15th-order polynomial versus 2nd- and 15th-order fits across training-set sizes.
- Fig 7, p.12: mode connectivity of two independently trained ResNet-164 on CIFAR-100, adapted from Garipov et al. 2018.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. The extraction is clean text. Math in the formulas (Eqs 1-6, Table 1) is scrambled, and the Appendix D penalty "P j 0.012j2w2j" is ambiguous. The Fig 1 and Fig 5 plot values are not recoverable as text. Fig 1(d) and (e) show axis tick values only, not the actual error numbers. The first Read of the persisted extraction was cut at about char 36500, so I re-read the rest with pypdf directly. Nothing was lost.
